quiz.q:
Where does the line beat the brake?

Problem. A six-bend profile 3 m long is quoted two ways. On a press brake each bend takes 6 s and handling adds 20 s per part, at a machine-and-operator rate of 60 per hour, on tooling costing 4,000. Roll formed, the line runs at 30 m/min at a rate of 90 per hour, on tooling costing 60,000. Find each route's parts per hour and cost per part, the break-even quantity, and what happens to it if the profile gains two more bends.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) Brake cycle \( =6(6)+20=56\ \mathrm{s} \), so \( 3600/56=64.3 \) parts per hour and \( 60/64.3=0.933 \) per part.

(2) Roll forming: at 30 m/min the line moves 0.5 m/s, so a 3 m part occupies it for 6 s — 600 parts per hour, and \( 90/600=0.150 \) per part. The line is \( 600/64.3=9.33 \) times faster.

(3) \( N^{*}=(60{,}000-4{,}000)/(0.933-0.150)=56{,}000/0.783=71{,}489 \) parts.

(4) Check: at that quantity both routes cost \( 60{,}000+71{,}489(0.150)=70{,}723 \) and \( 4{,}000+71{,}489(0.933)=70{,}723 \). Equal.

(5) Two more bends add \( 12\ \mathrm{s} \) to the brake cycle, making it 68 s: 52.9 parts an hour and 1.134 per part. The roll-formed rate is unchanged, though the tooling rises — say to 70,000 for two more stands. Then \( N^{*}=(70{,}000-4{,}000)/(1.134-0.150)=67{,}073 \) parts: the crossover falls despite the extra tooling.

Answer: 64.3 against 600 parts an hour, 0.933 against 0.150 per part, break-even 71,489; adding two bends lowers the crossover to about 67,000. Sanity check: the direction of the last result is the important one — bends cost time on a brake and only capital on a line, so a more complex profile favours roll forming even though its tooling gets dearer. Note what the number does not include: roll-forming tooling is profile-specific, so the quantity must be reached on one profile, and a changeover costs hours of line time that this arithmetic never sees.

quiz.q:
Why the leg edge waves, and how far to spread it

Problem. A 40 mm leg is raised from flat to vertical in a single 400 mm stand pitch, in mild steel with \( Y=250 \) MPa and \( E=207 \) GPa. Find the longitudinal strain forced on the leg edge, compare it with the yield strain, and say what defect results. Then find the forming length that keeps the edge elastic and the number of 300 mm stand pitches it implies.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) While the web travels \( L=400 \) mm along the line, the edge travels the hypotenuse of that length and its own rise: \( \sqrt{L^2+h^2} \).

(2) \( \varepsilon=\sqrt{1+(40/400)^2}-1=\sqrt{1.01}-1=0.004988 \), that is 0.499%.

(3) The yield strain is \( \varepsilon_y=Y/E=250/207{,}000=0.001208 \), or 0.121%.

(4) \( 0.499/0.121=4.13 \): the edge is strained four times past yield, so it lengthens permanently.

(5) A strip edge that is permanently longer than the strip has nowhere to go and buckles — edge wave, the ripple along the free edge of the finished section.

(6) Setting \( \varepsilon=\varepsilon_y \): \( L=h/\sqrt{(1+\varepsilon_y)^2-1}=40/0.04916=813.6\ \mathrm{mm} \).

(7) At a 300 mm stand pitch that is \( 813.6/300=2.71 \), so the leg must be raised over three stands, not one.

Answer: 0.499% against a 0.121% yield strain, 4.1 times over, producing edge wave; the bend needs 814 mm of forming length, three stands at a 300 mm pitch. Sanity check: the strain goes as \( h^2/2L^2 \), so it is far more sensitive to the leg height than to the pitch — doubling the leg to 80 mm would need four times the forming length, about 3.3 m, which is most of a line. That is the real reason deep-legged profiles need many stands, and it is decided on the flower pattern before any roll is cut rather than discovered on the line.

quiz.q:
Size the leveller

Problem. A 1.5 mm mild-steel coil (\( Y=250 \) MPa, \( E=207 \) GPa) arrives with coil set. To erase it, the leveller must strain the strip surface to five times its yield strain. Find the maximum leveller roll radius and diameter, and state what happens if larger rolls are used. Then find the roll radius needed for 3 mm sheet at the same criterion, and comment.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) Bending a strip of thickness \( t \) over a radius \( R \) strains its surface by \( \varepsilon=t/2R \).

(2) \( \varepsilon_y=250/207{,}000=0.001208 \), so the target is \( 5\varepsilon_y=0.006039 \).

(3) \( R=t/(2\varepsilon)=1.5/(2\times0.006039)=124.2\ \mathrm{mm} \), a diameter of 248.4 mm. Rolls must be that size or smaller, since a smaller radius gives more strain.

(4) With larger rolls the strain never reaches five times yield, so only the outer fibres yield and the core keeps its memory: the strip leaves the leveller looking flat and retains the residual stress that later shows up as bow or twist in the formed profile.

(5) For 3 mm at the same criterion, \( R=3/(2\times0.006039)=248.4\ \mathrm{mm} \) — the radius scales directly with thickness.

Answer: \( R\le124.2 \) mm (248.4 mm diameter) for 1.5 mm strip, and 248.4 mm radius for 3 mm; larger rolls leave residual stress that reappears as bow or twist. Sanity check: the linear scaling is worth noticing, because it says a leveller built for thin gauge is over-specified for thick and a leveller built for thick gauge simply cannot level thin — which is why lines carry roll cassettes rather than one set. Note also what levelling does not fix: camber from slitting is an in-plane curve, and rolls that bend the strip through its thickness do nothing about it.

quiz.q: On a roll-forming line, adding two more bends to a profile
choices: adds stands and tooling cost but leaves parts per hour unchanged
requires a second pass through the line
quiz.solution: The line runs at metres per minute regardless of how many stands it has, so complexity is paid for in capital rather than in time. On a brake the same two bends add 12 s to every cycle. That asymmetry is why extra bends push the break-even quantity down, toward roll forming, even though the tooling gets dearer.

quiz.q: For a six-bend 3 m profile, roll forming overtakes brake bending at about
quiz.solution: \( N^{*}=(60{,}000-4{,}000)/(0.933-0.150)=71{,}489 \). Below it the brake's cheap tooling wins despite being 9.3 times slower; above it the line's 0.15 per part does. The crossover is computable before either tool is ordered.

quiz.q: A flower pattern is
choices: the arrangement of parts on the coil
the cross-section superimposed at every stand
the wear pattern on the rolls
the layout of the cooling system
quiz.solution: It is the roll former's design document: every stand's section drawn on one set of axes, opening progressively. It encodes the angle schedule, the path the material takes — which is where edge strain is checked — and which surfaces stay flat enough to drive the strip.

quiz.q: Raising a 40 mm leg over a 400 mm forming length strains the leg edge about
choices: not at all — bending is a transverse operation
quiz.solution: \( \varepsilon=\sqrt{1+(40/400)^2}-1=0.499\% \). The edge must travel the hypotenuse while the web travels the base, and on a continuous strip that extra length can only come from stretching. Bending is transverse, but roll forming is bending while moving, which is what creates the longitudinal component.

quiz.q: Edge wave in a roll-formed section is caused by
choices: the rolls being set too tight
the leg edge being strained past yield, so it is permanently longer than the strip
quiz.solution: A permanently lengthened edge on a strip of fixed length has nowhere to go and buckles into a ripple. The cure is geometric rather than mechanical: spread the same bend over more forming length. Keeping \( \varepsilon\le\varepsilon_y \) for a 40 mm leg needs 814 mm, or three stands at a 300 mm pitch.

quiz.q: A leveller erases coil set by
choices: bending it alternately past yield over small-radius rolls
quiz.solution: The strip must be worked past yield in both directions until its residual curvature is erased, and that needs \( t/2R \) to reach several times the yield strain: rolls of 248 mm diameter or less for 1.5 mm mild steel. Larger rolls yield only the outer fibres, leaving a strip that looks flat and later bows.

quiz.q: End flare on roll-formed lengths occurs because
choices: the cut ends lose the restraint the continuous strip provided
the line accelerates at the cut
quiz.solution: While the strip is continuous, each section is held in shape by the material ahead of and behind it. Cutting removes that, and the free ends spring toward their unrestrained shape. The usual answers are to cut before forming, to trim a short scrap end, or to add a restraining stand close to the shear.

quiz.q: Which of these is not achievable by conventional roll forming?
choices: a 12 m length with six bends
a section whose shape changes along its length
a nearly closed section finished by seam welding
a profile with punched holes in line
quiz.solution: Every stand sees the same shape pass through it, so the section is constant along the length by construction. Long lengths, in-line punching and nearly closed sections completed by welding are all routine — the last because a fully closed profile would lose the driven flat surfaces the line needs to feed it.

4.kuwait:
Applied case — the profile that waved along one edge. A panel line was retooled for a new section with a 40 mm return leg, and the first production run came off with a visible ripple along that leg on every length. The rolls were checked, reset and checked again; the strip supplier was asked to confirm the coil's flatness; nothing changed.

The defect was designed in, not set up wrong. The flower pattern raised the leg from flat to vertical between two stands 400 mm apart, which forces the leg edge to travel \( \sqrt{400^2+40^2} \) while the web travels 400 — a longitudinal strain of 0.499% against a yield strain of 0.121%. The edge was being stretched four times past yield on every metre of strip, so it left the line permanently longer than the material beside it and buckled. No roll setting can absorb that, because the extra length is real. Keeping the edge elastic needs 814 mm of forming length, which at the line's 300 mm stand pitch meant raising the leg over three stands instead of one.

Two practices follow. Check the edge-strain criterion on the flower pattern before any roll is cut — it costs one line of arithmetic per leg and it is the commonest reason a new profile misbehaves. And when a defect appears identically on every part from the first metre onward, treat the design as the suspect rather than the setup: setup errors drift, wander and respond to adjustment, while a geometric impossibility does none of those things.
4.recap:
• Roll forming makes every bend at once on a strip that never stops, so profile complexity costs stands and capital rather than cycle time.
  • The crossover is computable: \( N^{*}=\Delta C/\Delta c \), here \( 56{,}000/0.783=71{,}489 \) parts for a six-bend 3 m profile.
  • Adding bends lowers the crossover, because they cost time on a brake and only capital on a line.
  • The flower pattern superimposes the section at every stand and encodes the angle schedule (15–30° a stand in mild steel, 3–8° in high-strength), the material path and the driven surfaces.
  • A rising leg forces longitudinal strain on its edge: \( \varepsilon=\sqrt{1+(h/L)^2}-1\approx h^2/2L^2 \).
  • A 40 mm leg over one 400 mm pitch gives 0.499% against a 0.121% yield strain — four times over, so the edge lengthens permanently and buckles into edge wave.
  • Keeping it elastic needs \( L\ge814 \) mm, three stands at a 300 mm pitch; the strain goes as \( h^2 \), so an 80 mm leg would need four times the length.
  • Levelling erases coil set only if \( t/2R \) reaches several times yield: rolls of 248 mm diameter or less for 1.5 mm steel, scaling linearly with thickness.
  • Slitting brings burr direction and camber; camber becomes bow in the finished profile and levelling does not fix it.
  • Sections hold \( \pm0.5 \) mm and \( \pm1^{\circ} \) but bow, camber and twist are hard; end flare is intrinsic; and the process cannot make a section that changes along its length.

5.lecture:
§1 · Two ways to push, and why the choice is not about size

A mechanical press stores energy in a flywheel and releases it through a clutch to a crank or eccentric that drives the slide. The slide's position is a fixed function of crank angle, so the stroke length, the velocity profile and the timing are all built into the machine and cannot be changed. A hydraulic press drives the slide with a cylinder, so force, speed, stroke length and dwell are all set by the control valve.

The distinction that matters is not force or size but where in the stroke the force is available. A crank converts torque to force with a mechanical advantage that depends on crank angle.

Key relation — slide force from crank torque

\[ F=\frac{T}{R\sin\theta},\qquad \cos\theta=1-\frac{s}{R} \]

\( R \) is the crank radius, \( \theta \) the angle from bottom dead centre and \( s \) the distance the slide is above BDC. As \( \theta\to0 \) the available force diverges, so a press's rating has to be quoted at a stated distance above BDC.

Take a 100-tonne press with a 100 mm stroke, so \( R=50 \) mm, rated at 6 mm above bottom dead centre. At that point \( \sin\theta=0.475 \). Twelve millimetres up, \( \sin\theta=0.650 \) and the available force is \( 0.475/0.650=73\% \) of the rating. At 25 mm it is 55%. At mid-stroke it is 47%.

So the answer to where each press wins is arithmetic rather than preference. Blanking and piercing finish at the bottom of the stroke and need force only there, so a mechanical press gives its whole rating and its 60–150 strokes a minute. Deep drawing needs force from the moment the punch touches the blank and holds it for the length of the draw, which is high in the stroke — so that 100-tonne press is a 55-tonne press for the job. The drawing operation of Lesson 3 needs 347 kN at that height, which 538 kN covers, but by a factor of 1.55 rather than the 2.8 the nameplate suggests, and the blankholder load arrives higher still where less is available. A hydraulic press delivers its rating anywhere, at any speed, with a dwell if the process wants one; it simply cannot match a mechanical press's cycle rate.

§2 · The die set and the progressive die

A die set is the frame that holds punch and die in register: two shoes joined by guide pillars and bushes, with the punch holder above and the die block below. Its specification follows directly from Lesson 1's clearance. If the guiding lets the punch wander by \( e \), the clearance becomes \( c-e \) on one side and \( c+e \) on the other, and the burr goes with it.

For 3 mm steel, \( c=0.18 \) mm. Holding both sides within \( \pm20\% \) of nominal needs \( e\le0.036 \) mm — even then the worst case is a side-to-side ratio of \( 0.216/0.144=1.5 \). That single number justifies the whole cost of a guided die set, and it is why a die run in a press with worn gibs produces a burr on one side and not the other.

A progressive die strings several stations along one strip: the strip advances by a fixed pitch each stroke, each station performs one operation, and a finished part falls out on every stroke once the die is full. An eight-station die at 100 strokes a minute delivers its first part after eight strokes — 4.8 seconds — and 100 parts a minute thereafter. The strip is the conveyor, which is the source of both its speed and its cost: the carrier web has to survive being fed, located and stripped at every station, so a progressive layout uses noticeably more material than the single-station nesting of Lesson 1.

A transfer die moves parts between stations mechanically instead, with no carrier, which recovers that material and buys the freedom to make parts a strip could not carry — at the cost of a transfer mechanism and its timing.

§3 · The three ways presses are broken

Overloading away from bottom dead centre is the first, and it is the tonnage curve being ignored. The press's gauge and its nameplate both say 100 tonnes; the crankshaft does not care what the nameplate says, and it fails in torsion. Any operation working high in the stroke has to be checked against the curve rather than the rating.

Off-centre loading is the second. If the resultant load does not act through the slide's centre, the slide tips, and the gibs and bearings carry the moment. Presses are rated for a maximum off-centre distance, and two dies of unequal tonnage sharing one bolster is the classic way to exceed it. The fix is layout: balance the tonnage about the centre, or accept a lower total.

Snap-through is the third and the least expected. Under load the press frame stretches elastically and stores energy; at the instant the blank fractures, the load vanishes and that energy is released in milliseconds.

Key relation — stored energy released at fracture

\[ \delta=\frac{F}{k},\qquad E=\tfrac12 k\delta^{2}=\frac{F^{2}}{2k} \]

A frame of stiffness 2,000 kN/mm carrying 1,000 kN stretches 0.5 mm and stores 250 J, all of which is dumped into the machine when the cut breaks through. The resulting reverse tonnage runs at 10–15% of the forward load and cracks frames and tie rods.

Everything that softens the breakthrough softens this: the angular shear of Lesson 1, staggered punch lengths so stations do not all break through together, and slower speeds on thick or hard material. It is the same physics as a bolt cutter kicking when the wire parts, at a scale that breaks castings.

§4 · Die maintenance is a scheduling problem, not a virtue

Punch and die edges wear round. A rounded edge behaves exactly like excessive clearance — heavier rollover, a bigger burr, more force — so Lesson 1's edge zones are the wear gauge, and burr height is the maintenance signal. Sharpening grinds the punch face back by two or three tenths of a millimetre and restores it; a punch with 12 mm of grindable length at 0.3 mm a sharpen has 40 sharpens in it, so at 200,000 hits between them its life is eight million hits.

Choosing the interval is the same problem Metrology & Quality Control solved for calibration. Sharpening costs a planned stoppage. Running too long costs an unplanned one, which is far worse: stripping, repairing and re-setting a crashed die takes hours where a sharpening takes three-quarters of one, and it scraps the parts in the die and sometimes damages the press. Measure both in the currency the line understands — parts of lost output — and the maintenance event costs about 4,500 while a crash costs about 24,000, a ratio of 5.3.

Key relation — the sharpening interval

\[ \text{cost per hit}=\frac{C_m}{N}+\frac{\lambda N C_c}{2}, \qquad N^{*}=\sqrt{\frac{2C_m}{\lambda C_c}} \]

\( N \) is the interval in hits, \( C_m \) the cost of a planned maintenance event, \( C_c \) the cost of a crash and \( \lambda \) the hazard rate, which grows with hits since the last sharpening.

With \( \lambda=10^{-11} \) per hit squared, \( N^{*}=194{,}000 \) hits — which is where shop practice sits, and the arithmetic recovers the rule of thumb rather than contradicting it. At the optimum the two cost terms are equal, exactly as they were for the calibration interval, and that equality is the fastest way to audit an existing schedule: if planned stoppages dominate the cost, the interval is too short, and if crashes do, it is too long.

Which is the answer to why die maintenance is a production indicator rather than a housekeeping one. It is not that maintained dies are tidier. It is that the interval is a decision with a computable cost, the wrong interval is expensive in both directions, and the evidence needed to set it — hits since sharpening, burr height, crash history — is data a shop either records or does not.

quiz.q:
Read the tonnage curve before choosing the press

Problem. A 100-tonne mechanical press has a 100 mm stroke and is rated 6 mm above bottom dead centre. Find the available force at 12 mm and at 25 mm above BDC, in tonnes and kilonewtons. The drawing operation of Lesson 3 needs 347 kN and must have it from 25 mm above BDC. Say whether this press can do the job, and what would.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) The crank radius is half the stroke, \( R=50 \) mm, and \( \cos\theta=1-s/R \), so \( \sin\theta=\sqrt{2s/R-(s/R)^2} \).

(2) At the rating point, \( s=6 \): \( \sin\theta=\sqrt{0.24-0.0144}=0.4750 \).

(3) At \( s=12 \): \( \sin\theta=\sqrt{0.48-0.0576}=0.6499 \), so the available fraction is \( 0.4750/0.6499=0.731 \) — 73.1 tonnes, or 717 kN.

(4) At \( s=25 \): \( \sin\theta=\sqrt{1.0-0.25}=0.8660 \), giving \( 0.4750/0.8660=0.548 \) — 54.8 tonnes, or 538 kN.

(5) The draw needs 347 kN at 25 mm, and 538 kN is available, so the press can supply the force — but with only a 1.55 factor over the requirement, and the machine's gauge and nameplate both suggest 981 kN, which is 2.8 times the truth at that height.

(6) The right machine is hydraulic: full rating anywhere in the stroke, adjustable ram speed, and a dwell at the bottom if the process wants one. A mechanical press would be the right answer for the blanking that produced the disc, which finishes at the bottom of the stroke.

Answer: 73.1 t (717 kN) at 12 mm and 54.8 t (538 kN) at 25 mm; the press can just do the 347 kN draw, at 55% of its nameplate, and a hydraulic press is the correct choice for drawing. Sanity check: the curve is steepest exactly where operations that matter live — between 6 and 25 mm the available force nearly halves — so a press chosen on its nameplate for a drawing job is routinely a press chosen at twice its real capacity. Note that the operation, not the part, decides: the same press is fully rated for blanking the blank and half-rated for drawing it.

quiz.q:
Guiding, and the energy that arrives after the cut

Problem. (a) A die blanks 3 mm steel at a clearance of 0.18 mm per side. Find the maximum punch-to-die wander the die set may allow if both sides are to stay within \( \pm20\% \) of nominal clearance, and the worst-case ratio between the two sides. (b) The same press has a frame stiffness of 2,000 kN/mm and the operation peaks at 1,000 kN. Find the frame's elastic stretch, the energy stored in it, and say what happens to that energy at breakthrough and what reduces it.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) Wander \( e \) makes the clearance \( c-e \) on one side and \( c+e \) on the other, so \( \pm20\% \) requires \( e\le0.20(0.18)=0.036\ \mathrm{mm} \).

(2) Even at that limit the sides are \( 0.144 \) and \( 0.216 \) mm, a ratio of \( 0.216/0.144=1.5 \) — so one side of every part carries a visibly heavier burr than the other.

(3) \( \delta=F/k=1000/2000=0.5\ \mathrm{mm} \) of elastic stretch in the frame.

(4) \( E=\tfrac12k\delta^{2}=\tfrac12(2000)(0.25)=250\ \mathrm{kN\,mm}=250\ \mathrm{J} \).

(5) At the instant the blank fractures the load vanishes and the frame recoils, releasing all 250 J in milliseconds. The resulting reverse tonnage is typically 10–15% of the forward load and is what cracks frames and breaks tie rods.

(6) Anything that makes the breakthrough gradual reduces it: angular shear on the tool, staggered punch lengths so stations do not break through together, and lower press speeds on thick or hard material.

Answer: \( e\le0.036 \) mm with a worst-case 1.5:1 side-to-side clearance ratio; 0.5 mm of frame stretch storing 250 J, released as reverse tonnage at breakthrough and softened by angular shear, staggered punches and slower speeds. Sanity check: both halves of this problem are the same idea — a press and die are elastic structures, and their deflections are of the same order as the clearances they are supposed to hold. Note that 0.036 mm is tighter than most people's mental image of a press tool, and that \( E=F^2/2k \) means a stiffer frame stores less energy at the same load, which is why heavy frames both deflect less and snap through less violently.

quiz.q:
Set the sharpening interval

Problem. A planned sharpening costs about 4,500 parts of lost output; an unplanned die crash costs about 24,000. The hazard of a crash grows with hits since the last sharpening, at \( \lambda=10^{-11} \) per hit squared. Find the cost per hit as a function of the interval, the optimum interval, the cost there, and the punch's total life if it has 12 mm of grindable length at 0.3 mm a sharpen. Comment on how to audit an existing interval without redoing the calculation.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) One maintenance event per \( N \) hits costs \( C_m/N \) per hit.

(2) If the hazard rises linearly with hits since sharpening, the expected crashes over an interval are \( \int_0^N\lambda x\,dx=\lambda N^2/2 \), which is \( \lambda N/2 \) per hit, costing \( \lambda NC_c/2 \).

(3) Total per hit: \( K(N)=C_m/N+\lambda NC_c/2 \).

(4) \( dK/dN=-C_m/N^2+\lambda C_c/2=0 \) gives \( N^{*}=\sqrt{2C_m/(\lambda C_c)}=\sqrt{9000/(2.4\times10^{-7})} =\sqrt{3.75\times10^{10}} \), so \( N^{*}=194{,}000 \) hits.

(5) \( K(N^{*})=4500/193{,}649+10^{-11}(193{,}649)(24{,}000)/2=0.0232+0.0232 =0.0465 \) parts of lost output per hit.

(6) Punch life: \( 12/0.3=40 \) sharpens, so \( 40\times194{,}000\approx7.7 \) million hits — about eight million at the round 200,000 interval shops use.

(7) To audit an interval without recomputing: at the optimum the two terms are equal. If planned stoppages dominate the maintenance cost, the interval is too short; if crashes dominate, it is too long.

Answer: \( K(N)=C_m/N+\lambda NC_c/2 \), minimised at \( N^{*}=194{,}000 \) hits costing 0.0465 parts per hit, with the two terms equal; the punch lasts 40 sharpens, roughly eight million hits. Sanity check: the arithmetic lands on the 200,000-hit interval shops already use, which is the right kind of agreement — the model recovers accumulated practice rather than overturning it, and its value is that it says why, and what to change when the costs change. Note that the whole structure is Metrology & Quality Control's calibration-interval problem with different labels: a planned cost that falls with the interval, an unplanned one that rises, and equality at the optimum.

quiz.solution: \( F=T/(R\sin\theta) \) diverges as the crank approaches bottom dead centre, so the available force depends entirely on where in the stroke it is measured. A 100-tonne press rated at 6 mm above BDC gives 73 tonnes at 12 mm and 55 at 25. A rating without its measuring point is not a specification.

quiz.solution: \( \sin\theta \) is 0.475 at the rating point and 0.866 at 25 mm, so the available fraction is \( 0.475/0.866=0.548 \) — 54.8 tonnes. The nameplate and the gauge both still say 100, which is why an operation working high in the stroke is the classic way to break a crankshaft.

hold punch-to-die register far tighter than the clearance

The strip is the conveyor, which is where the speed comes from and also why a progressive layout uses more material than the single-station nesting of Lesson 1.

choices: elastic energy stored in the press frame being released when the cut breaks through

The reverse load runs at 10–15% of the forward one and cracks frames and tie rods. Angular shear, staggered punch lengths and lower speeds all soften it.

quiz.q: The practical signal that a punch needs sharpening is

quiz.solution: A worn edge behaves like excessive clearance, so the burr grows — which makes Lesson 1's edge zones the wear gauge, readable on the parts without stopping the press. Stroke count sets the planned interval; burr height is what confirms or corrects it.

quiz.solution: Setting \( dK/dN=0 \) gives \( C_m/N=\lambda NC_c/2 \). It is the fastest audit of an existing schedule: if planned stoppages dominate the cost, the interval is too short; if crashes dominate, it is too long. 5.kuwait:
Applied case — the press that was chosen from its nameplate. A shop moved a drawing operation onto a 100-tonne mechanical press because the calculation said the job needed 347 kN — 35 tonnes — and the press had three times that. The first shift produced sound parts. Within a month the press was making an intermittent knock at the bottom of the stroke, and the crankshaft was found cracked at a journal fillet.

The force calculation was right and the press selection was not. The draw needs its force from the moment the punch touches the blank, about 25 mm above bottom dead centre, and at that height the crank's mechanical advantage gives \( \sin\theta=0.866 \) against the 0.475 at the 6 mm rating point: \( 0.475/0.866=55\% \) of the nameplate, or 538 kN. The job at 347 kN was inside that, but only by a factor of 1.55 rather than the 2.8 the nameplate implied — and the blankholder, whose force Lesson 3 put at 146 kN, arrives earlier still, higher in the stroke, where the available force is lower again. The machine was being worked near its real limit every stroke, and the failure was in torsion at the crankshaft, which is where a mechanical press fails when the load is applied where the crank has no advantage.

Two practices follow. Size a mechanical press against its tonnage curve at the height where the operation actually needs the force, never against the nameplate — the two differ by a factor of two over the range where real operations live. And treat operation type as a machine-selection criterion in its own right: blanking finishes at bottom dead centre and belongs on a mechanical press, while drawing needs force throughout the stroke and belongs on a hydraulic one, whatever the force numbers alone suggest.

  • Snap-through releases \( E=F^2/2k \) — 250 J at 1,000 kN on a 2,000 kN/mm frame — as 10–15% reverse tonnage; angular shear, staggered punches and slower speeds soften it.
  • Burr height is the wear gauge; a punch with 12 mm of grindable length at 0.3 mm a sharpen has 40 sharpens, roughly eight million hits.
  • The sharpening interval is a computable optimum, \( N^{*}=\sqrt{2C_m/\lambda C_c}=194{,}000 \) hits, where the two cost terms are equal — the same structure as a calibration interval.

6.lecture:
§1 · The screw is a pump that melts on the way

A single-screw extruder does three jobs with one rotating part. Solid pellets are dragged forward by the feed section, compacted and melted in the compression section as the channel depth shallows, and pumped at a steady rate through the metering section into the die. Almost all the melting energy is mechanical — the barrel heaters mostly hold temperature rather than supply it — which is why extruder output and melt temperature are coupled to screw speed and cannot be set independently.

The metering section is where the pumping happens, and it does two opposite things at once. The barrel surface moving relative to the screw drags melt forward; the pressure the die imposes pushes melt back down the channel.

Key relations — the screw characteristic

\[ Q_{\text{drag}}=\tfrac12\pi^{2}D^{2}NH\sin\phi\cos\phi,\qquad Q_{\text{back}}=\frac{\pi DH^{3}\sin^{2}\phi}{12\eta L}\,\Delta P \]

so \( Q=A-B\,\Delta P \). Drag flow depends on screw speed and channel depth; back flow depends on the cube of the depth and inversely on viscosity, which is why a shallow metering section makes a stiff pump.

For a 60 mm screw at 60 rev/min with a 3 mm metering depth, a square-pitch helix angle of 17.66° and a melt viscosity of 500 Pa·s, \( A=15.40\ \mathrm{cm^3/s} \) and \( B=1.30\times10^{-13}\ \mathrm{m^3/(s\,Pa)} \) — so 40 MPa of die pressure costs about a third of the drag flow.

§2 · Where the machine actually operates

The die is the other half of the system, and it behaves like a resistance: the more melt you push through it, the more pressure it takes.

Key relation — the die characteristic and the operating point

\[ Q=\frac{K}{\eta}\Delta P,\qquad K=\frac{\pi R^{4}}{8L_d},\qquad \Delta P^{*}=\frac{A}{B+K/\eta} \]

\( K \) is the die's conductance and \( R^{4} \) is why die size dominates it. Setting the two characteristics equal gives the one pressure and flow at which the machine runs.

Put a \( \varnothing5 \) mm die with a 20 mm land on that screw: \( K=7.67\times10^{-10} \), and the operating point is 9.26 MPa at 14.20 cm³/s — 47.5 kg an hour in polyethylene. Change to a \( \varnothing4 \) mm die and \( K \) falls by \( (4/5)^{4}=0.41 \), so the pressure climbs to 20.3 MPa while the output drops only to 12.76 cm³/s.

That asymmetry — the pressure more than doubles and the output falls a tenth — is the practically important reading of the diagram. A single-screw extruder is a stiff pump, so anything that restricts the flow path shows up in the pressure gauge long before it shows up in the throughput. A blinding screen pack, a die chilling at one edge and a degraded melt all announce themselves the same way, which is why head pressure is the number an extruder operator watches.

§3 · Die swell, and what it tells you about the melt

Extrude through a 4 mm die and the strand that emerges is not 4 mm. It is larger — often 20 to 50% larger — and it got that way in the first few millimetres after the die lip.

Key relation — the swell ratio

\[ B=\frac{D_{\text{extrudate}}}{D_{\text{die}}},\qquad B\approx1+(B_0-1)\,e^{-t/\lambda},\qquad t=\frac{L_d}{v} \]

\( \lambda \) is the melt's relaxation time and \( t \) the residence time in the die land. Swell falls as the melt is given time to forget.

What die swell reveals is that a polymer melt is viscoelastic, not a viscous liquid. In the converging entry to the die the chains are stretched and oriented; in the land they begin to relax; on exit, whatever elastic strain is left recovers, and the extrudate expands. A Newtonian fluid does not do this at all.

Which makes swell a design variable rather than a nuisance. At 14.20 cm³/s through a \( \varnothing5 \) die the melt velocity in the land is 0.72 m/s, so a 20 mm land gives 27.7 ms of relaxation — about a quarter of a 100 ms relaxation time, so most of the elastic strain survives and the swell is 1.38. Lengthen the land to 100 mm and the residence time reaches 138 ms, more than one relaxation time, and the swell falls to 1.13. The other levers work the same way: higher temperature shortens \( \lambda \), higher shear rate raises \( B_0 \), and a long land costs pressure because \( K\propto1/L_d \).

The practical consequence is that the die is never the product size. A 5 mm strand at a swell of 1.25 needs a 4 mm die; and since the die is cut before the material is fully characterised, first articles are a measurement exercise rather than a formality.

§4 · Downstream, and why cable is extruded rather than moulded

What leaves the die is hot, soft and oversize. Everything after it is a line: a sizing device fixing the outside dimension while the skin is still forming, a cooling bath, a haul-off that pulls the product through at a controlled speed, and a cutter or coiler.

The haul-off is a process variable, not just a conveyor. Pulling faster than the melt emerges draws the extrudate down, and the area ratio is the square of the diameter ratio: taking a 5 mm free extrudate to a 3 mm product is a drawdown of \( (5/3)^{2}=2.78 \). So the finished size is set by the die, the swell and the haul-off together, and only one of the three is fixed in steel.

The cooling bath's length is a heat-transfer calculation, not a guess. For a 3 mm strand of thermal diffusivity \( 10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m^2/s} \) cooled in water, the centre reaches within 5% of the bath temperature at a Fourier number of about 0.60, so \( t=0.60R^{2}/\alpha=13.5\ \mathrm{s} \) — which at a line speed of 1 m/s means 13.5 metres of bath. Double the line speed and the bath doubles; that is why extrusion halls are long.

All of which explains the question about cable. Insulation is applied by pulling the conductor through a crosshead die that turns the melt through 90° and wraps it round the moving wire. It is done that way for one decisive reason and two supporting ones. The decisive one is continuity: a cable is kilometres long and every joint in its insulation is an electrical weak point, so a process with a defined part length is disqualified before cost is discussed.

The supporting reasons are rate and control. A 1.4 mm conductor insulated to 2.8 mm carries \( \frac{\pi}{4}(2.8^{2}-1.4^{2})=4.62\ \mathrm{mm^{2}} \) of polymer, so at 300 m/min the line consumes 23.1 cm³/s, or 77 kg an hour — a continuous demand no batch process serves. Our 60 mm extruder at 14.20 cm³/s would run the same cable at 184 m/min, and that arithmetic is the coupling that matters: output and line speed are one variable. A 1% drift in extruder output is a 1% error in wall thickness, which is why the wall is measured continuously in line rather than on samples, and why the insulation wall — not the conductor, which arrives already sized — is what the process actually controls.

quiz.q:
Find the operating point, then change the die

Problem. A 60 mm single-screw extruder runs at 60 rev/min with a 3 mm metering depth, a 600 mm metering length, a square-pitch helix angle of 17.66° and a melt viscosity of 500 Pa·s, giving \( A=15.40\ \mathrm{cm^3/s} \) and \( B=1.30\times10^{-13}\ \mathrm{m^3/(s\,Pa)} \). Find the operating pressure and output with a \( \varnothing5 \) mm die of 20 mm land, then repeat for a \( \varnothing4 \) mm die, and say what the comparison tells you about the machine.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) The die's conductance is \( K=\pi R^{4}/8L_d \). For \( R=2.5 \) mm and \( L_d=20 \) mm, \( K=\pi(2.5\times10^{-3})^{4}/(8\times0.02)=7.67\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m^3} \).

(2) The two characteristics are \( Q=A-B\Delta P \) and \( Q=(K/\eta)\Delta P \). Setting them equal, \( \Delta P^{*}=A/(B+K/\eta) \).

(3) \( K/\eta=7.67\times10^{-10}/500=1.534\times10^{-12} \), so \( \Delta P^{*}=1.540\times10^{-5}/(1.30\times10^{-13}+1.534\times10^{-12}) =9.26\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{Pa}=9.26\ \mathrm{MPa} \).

(4) \( Q=(K/\eta)\Delta P^{*}=1.42\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{m^3/s}=14.20\ \mathrm{cm^3/s} \), which in polyethylene at 930 kg/m³ is 47.5 kg an hour.

(5) For \( R=2.0 \) mm, \( K \) falls by \( (4/5)^{4}=0.410 \) to \( 3.14\times10^{-10} \), so \( K/\eta=6.28\times10^{-13} \) and \( \Delta P^{*}=1.540\times10^{-5}/(7.58\times10^{-13})=20.3\ \mathrm{MPa} \).

(6) \( Q=6.28\times10^{-13}(2.03\times10^{7})=1.276\times10^{-5}=12.76\ \mathrm{cm^3/s} \).

(7) The pressure rose by a factor of 2.19 while the output fell by only 10%.

Answer: 9.26 MPa at 14.20 cm³/s on the \( \varnothing5 \) die; 20.3 MPa at 12.76 cm³/s on the \( \varnothing4 \). The screw is a stiff pump. Sanity check: \( K\propto R^{4} \) makes the die by far the more sensitive half of the system, so a 20% smaller radius is a 59% smaller conductance — and the screw absorbs almost all of that in pressure rather than in flow. That is the practical reading: head pressure is a sensitive early indicator of a blinding screen pack or a chilling die, and throughput is a late one. Note also that neither the screw nor the die sets the output alone; only their intersection does.

quiz.q:
Size the die for the strand you want

Problem. A 5.0 mm strand is required. (a) If the melt's swell ratio is 1.25, what die opening is needed? (b) For the extruder above running 14.20 cm³/s through a \( \varnothing5 \) die, find the melt velocity in the land, and use \( B=1+(B_0-1)e^{-t/\lambda} \) with \( B_0=1.5 \) and \( \lambda=100 \) ms to find the swell at a 20 mm land and at a 100 mm land. (c) Give one cost of the longer land.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (a) The extrudate is \( B \) times the die, so the die must be \( 5.0/1.25=4.0\ \mathrm{mm} \).

(b1) Velocity in the land: \( v=Q/\pi R^{2}=1.42\times10^{-5}/(\pi(2.5\times10^{-3})^{2}) =1.42\times10^{-5}/1.963\times10^{-5}=0.723\ \mathrm{m/s} \).

(b2) A 20 mm land gives \( t=0.020/0.723=27.7\ \mathrm{ms} \), so \( t/\lambda=0.277 \) and \( B=1+0.5e^{-0.277}=1+0.5(0.758)=1.38 \).

(b3) A 100 mm land gives \( t=138\ \mathrm{ms} \), \( t/\lambda=1.383 \), and \( B=1+0.5e^{-1.383}=1+0.5(0.251)=1.13 \).

(c) The land is a resistance: \( K=\pi R^{4}/8L_d \), so five times the land is a fifth of the conductance — the operating pressure rises steeply and the output falls, exactly as in the previous problem's die change.

Answer: a 4.0 mm die for a 5.0 mm strand at \( B=1.25 \); melt velocity 0.723 m/s, swell 1.38 at a 20 mm land and 1.13 at 100 mm; the longer land costs pressure and output. Sanity check: the swell falls toward 1 as the residence time passes one relaxation time, which is the right limit — given long enough the melt forgets its history entirely and there is nothing elastic left to recover. Note what this means for tooling: the die opening depends on the material's relaxation behaviour, the land length and the throughput, none of which is known precisely before the first trial, so a production die is normally cut small and opened.

quiz.q:
Design the line around the cable

Problem. A 1.4 mm conductor is to be insulated to a 2.8 mm outside diameter. Find the insulation's cross-sectional area, the volumetric and mass rates at a line speed of 300 m/min in polyethylene at 930 kg/m³, and the line speed the 14.20 cm³/s extruder above would support. Then find the cooling-bath length for a 3 mm strand at 1 m/s, taking \( \alpha=10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m^2/s} \) and a Fourier number of 0.60.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) \( A=\frac{\pi}{4}(2.8^{2}-1.4^{2})=\frac{\pi}{4}(7.84-1.96)=\frac{\pi}{4}(5.88) =4.62\ \mathrm{mm^{2}} \).

(2) At 300 m/min \( =5 \) m/s: \( Q=4.62\times10^{-6}(5)=2.31\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{m^3/s}=23.1\ \mathrm{cm^3/s} \).

(3) Mass rate \( =2.31\times10^{-5}(930)(3600)=77.3\ \mathrm{kg/h} \).

(4) Our extruder gives \( 1.42\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{m^3/s} \), so the line speed it supports is \( 1.42\times10^{-5}/4.62\times10^{-6}=3.07\ \mathrm{m/s}=184\ \mathrm{m/min} \).

(5) Cooling: \( t=\mathrm{Fo}\,R^{2}/\alpha=0.60(1.5\times10^{-3})^{2}/10^{-7} =0.60(22.5)=13.5\ \mathrm{s} \).

(6) At 1 m/s that is 13.5 m of bath; at the cable line's 5 m/s it would be 67 m.

Answer: 4.62 mm² of insulation, 23.1 cm³/s and 77.3 kg/h at 300 m/min; the extruder supports 184 m/min; the bath is 13.5 m at 1 m/s. Sanity check: output and line speed are one variable, not two — which is the whole reason a cable line is speed-controlled from the extruder rather than the other way round, and why a 1% drift in output is a 1% wall-thickness error rather than a 1% length error. Note the bath result too: cooling time scales with \( R^{2} \) but bath length scales with speed as well, so doubling the line speed doubles the hall while doubling the strand diameter quadruples the time.

quiz.q: In a single-screw extruder, most of the energy that melts the polymer comes from
choices: mechanical work done by the screw
quiz.solution: Viscous dissipation and the work of dragging and compacting the solids do most of the melting; the barrel heaters largely hold temperature. That is why melt temperature rises with screw speed and cannot be set independently of output — a coupling that surprises anyone expecting an oven.

quiz.q: In the screw characteristic \( Q=A-B\Delta P \), the coefficient \( B \) is proportional to
choices: the square of the channel depth
the cube of the channel depth
quiz.solution: \( Q_{\text{back}}=\pi DH^{3}\sin^{2}\phi\,\Delta P/12\eta L \) — back flow is a pressure-driven flow in a shallow channel, so it goes as \( H^{3} \). A shallow metering section therefore makes a stiff pump whose output barely moves with die pressure, which is usually what an extruder wants.

quiz.q: An extruder's actual output is set by
choices: the intersection of the screw and die characteristics
quiz.solution: The screw's output falls with pressure and the die's rises with it, so exactly one pressure satisfies both: \( \Delta P^{*}=A/(B+K/\eta) \). It is the same construction as a pump meeting a system curve. The haul-off sets the drawdown, not the throughput.

quiz.q: Changing from a \( \varnothing5 \) mm die to a \( \varnothing4 \) mm die on the same screw
choices: halves the output and leaves the pressure alone
more than doubles the pressure and reduces output by about a tenth
quiz.solution: \( K\propto R^{4} \), so a 20% smaller radius is a 59% smaller conductance: the pressure goes 9.26 to 20.3 MPa while the output goes 14.20 to 12.76 cm³/s. The screw is a stiff pump, which is why head pressure is a sensitive early warning of a restriction and throughput is not.

quiz.q: Die swell shows that a polymer melt is
choices: viscoelastic, storing elastic strain that recovers on exit
quiz.solution: Chains stretched and oriented in the die's converging entry recover whatever elastic strain survives the land, so the extrudate expands. A purely viscous fluid shows no swell at all. Everything that gives the melt time to relax — a longer land, a higher temperature, a lower rate — reduces it.

quiz.q: Lengthening the die land from 20 mm to 100 mm takes the swell ratio from 1.38 to 1.13 because
choices: the residence time passes one relaxation time, so more elastic strain has relaxed
quiz.solution: At 0.723 m/s the land time goes from 27.7 to 138 ms against a 100 ms relaxation time, so \( e^{-t/\lambda} \) falls from 0.76 to 0.25. The cost is conductance: \( K\propto1/L_d \), so five times the land is a fifth of the conductance and a much higher operating pressure.

quiz.q: Cable insulation is extruded rather than moulded principally because
choices: a cable is continuous and every joint in its insulation is an electrical weak point
polymers cannot be moulded onto metal
quiz.solution: Continuity disqualifies any process with a defined part length before cost is discussed. Rate and control support it — a 2.8 mm cable at 300 m/min consumes 77 kg an hour continuously — but the decisive argument is that a joint in insulation is a defect, not an inconvenience.

quiz.q: On a cable line, a 1% drift in extruder output produces
choices: a 1% error in insulation wall thickness
no effect, since the haul-off compensates
quiz.solution: Output and line speed are one variable: the wall is whatever the melt rate divided by the line speed makes it. That is why the wall is gauged continuously in line rather than on samples, and why the process controls the insulation rather than the conductor, which arrives already sized.

6.kuwait:
Applied case — the die that was cut to the drawing. A cable line was retooled for a new insulation wall, and the crosshead die was cut to the finished outside diameter on the reasonable assumption that the die makes the part. First trials produced insulation consistently oversize by roughly a quarter, the haul-off was increased to pull it down, and the wall then varied along the length as the drawdown fought the swell.

The die was the wrong size by design. A polymer melt is viscoelastic: chains oriented in the die's entry recover on exit, so the extrudate leaves larger than the opening by the swell ratio \( B \), here about 1.25. A die intended to produce a 5.0 mm outside diameter had to be cut at \( 5.0/1.25=4.0 \) mm. Compensating with haul-off instead does something different — it draws the extrudate down while it is still molten, which orients it further and leaves the wall sensitive to every small variation in output, which is exactly the instability that was then observed.

Two practices follow. Size an extrusion die from the product size and the measured swell of that material at that rate and temperature, and treat the first article as the measurement that establishes \( B \) rather than as an inspection. And keep the two levers separate: swell is set by the die geometry and the melt's relaxation, drawdown by the haul-off, and using one to correct the other buys a dimension at the cost of stability.

7.lecture:
§1 · The cycle is mostly waiting for heat to leave

An injection moulding cycle runs: close the mould, inject melt to fill the cavity, hold pressure while the part shrinks so more melt can be packed in, cool until the part is rigid enough to handle, open, eject. Filling takes about a second. Cooling takes most of the rest, and it obeys a law with one enormously consequential feature.

Key relation — cooling time

\[ t_{\text{cool}}=\frac{h^{2}}{\pi^{2}\alpha} \ln\!\left[\frac{4}{\pi}\,\frac{T_m-T_w}{T_e-T_w}\right] \]

\( h \) is the wall thickness, \( \alpha \) the polymer's thermal diffusivity, \( T_m \) the melt, \( T_w \) the mould wall and \( T_e \) the ejection temperature. Thickness enters squared; every temperature enters only inside a logarithm.

For a 3 mm wall at 230°C melt, a 40°C mould and 90°C ejection, the logarithm is 1.58 and \( t_{\text{cool}}=14.4\ \mathrm{s} \). Add a second to fill, five to pack and three to open and eject, and the cycle is 23.4 s — 154 parts an hour.

Now halve the wall. Cooling falls to 3.6 s, packing shortens with it, and the cycle becomes 10.6 s: 340 parts an hour from the same machine and the same tool cavity count. That factor of 2.2 is why wall thickness is the first thing a moulding engineer looks at on a new drawing, and why "just make it thicker to be safe" is the most expensive sentence in plastic part design. Note also what the logarithm implies: running the mould colder or the melt hotter changes the cycle hardly at all, because those live inside a log while thickness is squared outside it.

§2 · Sizing the machine, and what the gate decides

Two numbers select a moulding machine. Clamp force must exceed the cavity pressure acting over the projected area, or the mould opens against it.

Key relation — clamp force

\[ F=p_{\text{cav}}\,A_{\text{proj}} \]

\( A_{\text{proj}} \) is the part's area projected onto the parting plane, including runners. Cavity pressures of 20–50 MPa are typical.

A 150 × 100 mm plate at 35 MPa needs \( 35\times15{,}000=525\ \mathrm{kN} \), 53.5 tonnes, so a 65-tonne machine with margin. The other number is shot size: 45 cm³ of part plus about 12 cm³ of sprue and runner, and a machine should use roughly a fifth to four-fifths of its shot capacity — too little and the melt sits degrading in the barrel, too much and there is no cushion to pack with.

The gate is the small restriction where melt enters the cavity, and its size sets something that is easy to miss: how long you are allowed to pack. A gate is just a thin section, so it obeys the same cooling law, and once it freezes no more melt can enter however hard the machine pushes.

A 1.0 mm gate freezes in 1.6 s. A 2.0 mm gate takes 6.4 s — four times as long, by the same square law. So a small gate degates cleanly and leaves a neat witness mark, and it closes the packing window that controls shrinkage; a large gate packs well and leaves a scar someone has to trim. That is the trade, and it is quantitative rather than a matter of taste.

Between sprue and gate sits the runner. A cold runner solidifies with the part and is scrap — 12 cm³ against a 45 cm³ part is 21% of every shot, recoverable as regrind only where the application allows it. A hot runner keeps the melt molten right up to the gate, so there is no runner at all, at the price of a much more expensive and more temperamental tool. The choice is the same fixed-versus-variable crossover as Lesson 4's.

§3 · Shrinkage is easy; differential shrinkage is the problem

Polymers shrink as they cool, and semi-crystalline grades shrink far more than amorphous ones — 1.5 to 2.5% linear for polypropylene and polyethylene against 0.4 to 0.7% for polystyrene or ABS — because crystallising packs the chains closer.

Key relation — cutting the mould oversize

\[ L_{\text{mould}}=\frac{L_{\text{part}}}{1-s} \]

A 150 mm feature in polypropylene at \( s=1.5\% \) needs the steel cut at 152.28 mm. Uniform shrinkage is a tooling calculation, and a solved problem.

What is not solved is differential shrinkage, because a part that shrinks unevenly does not come out smaller — it comes out bent. Three things make shrinkage uneven: wall thickness varying across the part, cooling reaching one face faster than the other, and orientation.

Orientation is the one that answers why gate location decides warpage. Melt flowing into a cavity aligns its molecules — and, in a filled grade, its fibres — along the flow direction. Aligned fibres restrain shrinkage along the flow and do nothing about it across the flow, so shrinkage becomes anisotropic: a 30% glass-filled polypropylene might shrink 0.3% along the flow and 0.9% across it, a factor of three.

On a 150 mm square plate gated at one edge, that is 0.45 mm of shrinkage along the flow against 1.35 mm across it — a 0.9 mm differential, which the part resolves by bowing. Move the gate to the centre and the flow becomes radial, so the anisotropy becomes radial against hoop and the part dishes or saddles instead. The gate did not change the material or the shrinkage; it changed the flow field, and the flow field sets the orientation that sets the differential. That causal chain — gate, flow, orientation, differential shrinkage, warp — is why gate position is a structural decision rather than a convenience.

§4 · Reading the defects backwards

Moulding defects are diagnosable because each one is a specific failure of one phase of the cycle.

Short shot — the cavity did not fill. The melt either could not get there or ran out: too little shot volume, too little injection pressure or speed, melt too cold, a gate too small for the section, or a blocked vent leaving trapped air with nowhere to go. That last cause is worth naming, because it produces a short shot that no amount of extra pressure will fix.

Flash — melt escaped at the parting line, which means the mould opened. Either the clamp force was below \( p_{\text{cav}}A_{\text{proj}} \), or the injection pressure drove \( p_{\text{cav}} \) above what was assumed, or the parting-line steel is worn. On the worked part, a machine set at 450 kN against a 525 kN requirement will flash on every shot, and no process adjustment short of reducing pressure — which risks a short shot — will stop it.

Sink marks and voids — a region shrank after the surface had frozen and nothing fed it. The cause is almost always a local section thicker than the wall around it. A rib or boss joins the wall at a junction whose effective thickness is greater than either, and thickness is squared in the cooling law: a junction 1.3 times the wall thickness stays molten 1.69 times as long as the skin around it. Hence the design rule that a rib should be 0.5 to 0.6 of the wall — 1.8 mm on a 3 mm wall — and hence the process causes too: packing pressure or time too low, or a gate that froze before packing finished, which returns to \( \S2 \).

Weld lines form where two flow fronts meet, around a hole or between two gates, and carry 40 to 90% of the bulk strength depending on how hot the fronts still were. They cannot be eliminated where the part has a hole; they can be placed, by choosing the gate. Burn marks are trapped air compressed and ignited at the last point to fill, and are a venting problem rather than a temperature one. And warpage is \( \S3 \).

The pattern in all of this is that the cycle's phases map onto the defects one to one: filling failures give shorts and burns, clamping failures give flash, packing failures give sinks and voids, and cooling and orientation failures give warp. Diagnosing a moulding problem is mostly a matter of asking which phase the symptom belongs to before touching a setting.

quiz.q:
What the wall thickness is worth

Problem. A part is moulded from a 230°C melt into a 40°C mould and ejected at 90°C, with \( \alpha=10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m^2/s} \). Find the cooling time for a 3.0 mm wall and for a 1.5 mm wall. Taking 1 s to fill, 5 s of packing at 3 mm and 3 s at 1.5 mm, and 3 s to open and eject, find each cycle time and hourly rate. Then say what running the mould 10°C colder would do, and why.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) The logarithm is common to both: \( \ln[\frac{4}{\pi}\frac{230-40}{90-40}]=\ln[1.273(3.80)]=\ln(4.838)=1.577 \).

(2) At \( h=3.0 \) mm: \( t=\frac{(3\times10^{-3})^{2}}{\pi^{2}(10^{-7})}(1.577) =9.119(1.577)=14.4\ \mathrm{s} \).

(3) At \( h=1.5 \) mm: \( t=2.280(1.577)=3.6\ \mathrm{s} \) — a quarter, because thickness is squared.

(4) Cycles: \( 1+5+14.4+3=23.4\ \mathrm{s} \) and \( 1+3+3.6+3=10.6\ \mathrm{s} \).

(5) Rates: \( 3600/23.4=154 \) and \( 3600/10.6=340 \) parts an hour — a factor of 2.21.

(6) A 30°C mould instead of 40°C changes the logarithm to \( \ln[1.273(200/60)]=\ln(4.244)=1.445 \), so the 3 mm cooling time falls from 14.4 to 13.2 s — about 8%. Temperatures sit inside a logarithm and thickness sits outside it, squared, so geometry dominates and process settings barely move the cycle.

Answer: 14.4 s and 3.6 s of cooling, 23.4 s and 10.6 s cycles, 154 and 340 parts an hour; a 10°C colder mould buys about 8%. Sanity check: the two levers differ by an order of magnitude in effect, which is the whole economics of the process — a designer who halves the wall doubles the factory, and a process engineer who chills the mould gains a few per cent and risks freezing the gate early. Note that the packing time shortens with the wall too, so the cycle gain is slightly better than cooling alone suggests.

quiz.q:
Size the machine and choose the gate

Problem. A 150 × 100 × 3 mm plate is moulded at a cavity pressure of 35 MPa, with 12 cm³ of sprue and runner. Find the required clamp force in kilonewtons and tonnes, the shot volume, and the runner's share of it. Then find the packing window available with a 1.0 mm gate and with a 2.0 mm gate, and say which to choose for a part that must hold a tight dimension.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) Projected area \( =150\times100=15{,}000\ \mathrm{mm^2} \), so \( F=p_{\text{cav}}A_{\text{proj}}=35(15{,}000)=525{,}000\ \mathrm{N}=525\ \mathrm{kN} \).

(2) \( 525/9.81=53.5 \) tonnes, so a 65-tonne machine with sensible margin.

(3) Part volume \( =150(100)(3)=45{,}000\ \mathrm{mm^3}=45\ \mathrm{cm^3} \); shot \( =45+12=57\ \mathrm{cm^3} \).

(4) Runner share \( =12/57=21\% \) of every shot.

(5) A gate is a thin section obeying the same cooling law: a 1.0 mm gate freezes in \( 1.597\ \mathrm{s} \), a 2.0 mm gate in \( 6.390\ \mathrm{s} \) — four times longer, by the square.

(6) A tight dimension is held by packing, which compensates shrinkage, so the part needs the longer window: the 2.0 mm gate. The cost is a larger witness mark to trim and more sensitivity to the gate's own orientation effects.

Answer: 525 kN (53.5 t), a 57 cm³ shot of which the runner is 21%, packing windows of 1.6 s and 6.4 s; choose the 2.0 mm gate for dimensional control. Sanity check: the gate is the smallest feature in the tool and it governs the phase that controls shrinkage, which is a good example of a process where the least conspicuous dimension is the most consequential. Note the runner figure too: 21% of every shot is a material cost that recurs forever, and it is the number a hot-runner proposal has to beat.

quiz.q:
Why the plate bows, and what the gate has to do with it

Problem. A 150 mm square plate is moulded in a 30% glass-filled polypropylene that shrinks 0.3% along the flow and 0.9% across it. (a) Cut the mould for an unfilled polypropylene at 1.5% uniform shrinkage first, for comparison. (b) For the filled grade gated at one edge, find the shrinkage in each direction and the differential. (c) Explain what changes if the gate is moved to the centre. (d) A 3 mm wall carries a rib; give the maximum rib thickness and justify it from the cooling law.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (a) Uniform shrinkage is a tooling calculation: \( L_{\text{mould}}=150/(1-0.015)=152.28\ \mathrm{mm} \). Nothing warps, because every direction shrinks alike.

(b) Filled and edge-gated, the flow runs one way across the plate. Along the flow: \( 150(0.003)=0.45\ \mathrm{mm} \). Across it: \( 150(0.009)=1.35\ \mathrm{mm} \). The differential is \( 0.90\ \mathrm{mm} \), a factor of three between directions.

(c) A part cannot shrink by two different amounts and stay flat, so it bows. Moving the gate to the centre makes the flow radial: the anisotropy becomes radial against hoop, and the part dishes or saddles instead of bowing. The material, the shrinkage values and the wall are unchanged — only the flow field, and therefore the orientation, moved.

(d) Rib thickness \( \le0.5 \) to \( 0.6 \) of the wall, so \( \le1.8\ \mathrm{mm} \) on a 3 mm wall. The justification is the square law: a junction whose effective thickness is 1.3 times the wall stays molten \( 1.3^{2}=1.69 \) times as long as the skin around it, so it shrinks after the surface has frozen and pulls it in as a sink.

Answer: 152.28 mm of steel for the unfilled part; 0.45 and 1.35 mm of shrinkage with a 0.90 mm differential for the filled one; a centre gate converts a bow into a dish; ribs no thicker than 1.8 mm. Sanity check: uniform shrinkage is a solved problem and differential shrinkage is not, which is the distinction the whole subject turns on — and it explains why an unfilled part can be tooled from a table while a filled one usually needs a flow simulation. Note the causal chain in (c): the gate sets the flow, the flow sets the orientation, orientation sets the differential and the differential sets the warp, so gate position is a structural decision rather than a convenience.

quiz.q: In the cooling-time relation, wall thickness appears
quiz.solution: \( t=\frac{h^{2}}{\pi^{2}\alpha}\ln[\cdot] \) — thickness is squared outside, while every temperature sits inside the logarithm. That asymmetry is the economics of the process: halving the wall quarters the cooling, while a 10°C colder mould buys about 8%.

quiz.q: Halving a part's wall from 3.0 mm to 1.5 mm takes the hourly output from about
quiz.solution: Cooling falls from 14.4 to 3.6 s and packing shortens with it, so the cycle goes 23.4 to 10.6 s — 154 to 340 parts an hour, a factor of 2.21. It is not the full factor of four, because filling, opening and ejecting do not scale with the wall.

quiz.q: A 150 × 100 mm plate moulded at 35 MPa cavity pressure needs a clamp force of about
quiz.solution: \( F=p_{\rm cav}A_{\rm proj}=35\ \mathrm{MPa}\times15{,}000\ \mathrm{mm^2} =525\ \mathrm{kN} \), or 53.5 tonnes — the tonnes figure is the one that gets confused with the kilonewtons. A machine set below it flashes on every shot.

quiz.q: Gate size matters most because it sets
choices: how long packing can continue before the gate freezes
quiz.solution: A gate is a thin section obeying the same square law, so a 1.0 mm gate freezes in 1.6 s and a 2.0 mm gate in 6.4 s. Packing is what compensates shrinkage, so the gate silently decides how much dimensional control the process has — the smallest feature in the tool governing the most consequential phase.

quiz.q: A mould cavity for a 150 mm polypropylene part shrinking 1.5% should be cut at
quiz.solution: \( L_{\rm mould}=L_{\rm part}/(1-s)=150/0.985=152.28 \) mm. The common slip is \( 150\times1.015=152.25 \), which is close but wrong in principle: the part shrinks from the mould dimension, so the mould is the larger quantity being divided into, not the smaller one being scaled up.

quiz.q: Gate location decides warpage because it decides
choices: the flow field, which sets molecular and fibre orientation and hence the shrinkage differential
quiz.solution: Flow aligns molecules and fibres, aligned fibres restrain shrinkage along the flow but not across it, and a part that shrinks 0.3% one way and 0.9% the other cannot stay flat. An edge gate on a 150 mm plate gives a 0.9 mm differential and a bow; a centre gate makes the flow radial and turns the bow into a dish.

quiz.q: A sink mark on the surface opposite a rib is caused by
choices: the rib being thick enough that its junction stays molten after the surface has frozen
quiz.solution: Thickness is squared in the cooling law, so a junction 1.3 times the wall stays molten 1.69 times as long as the skin around it; it shrinks last, with nothing left to feed it, and pulls the surface in. Hence the rule that a rib is 0.5 to 0.6 of the wall — 1.8 mm on a 3 mm wall.

quiz.q: A part shows flash at the parting line on every shot. The cause is most likely
choices: clamp force below \( p_{\rm cav}A_{\rm proj} \), or injection pressure above what was assumed
quiz.solution: Flash means the mould opened, which is a force balance: the melt pushed harder over the projected area than the clamp held. On the worked part, 450 kN of clamp against a 525 kN requirement flashes every shot, and no setting short of reducing pressure — which risks a short shot — will stop it.

7.kuwait:
Applied case — the rib that was added for stiffness. A moulded housing was failing a deflection test, so the design was revised with a stiffening rib the same thickness as the wall — 3 mm on a 3 mm wall — on the reasonable ground that a thicker rib is a stiffer rib. The next tool produced parts with a visible sink line on the show surface directly opposite the rib, and a cycle time that had grown by several seconds.

Both effects came from the same square law. A rib as thick as the wall makes a junction whose effective thickness is roughly 1.3 times the wall, and cooling goes as thickness squared, so that junction stayed molten \( 1.3^{2}=1.69 \) times as long as the skin around it. It therefore shrank after the surface had frozen, with the gate long since closed and nothing able to feed it, and pulled the surface in. The same thick junction also set the cycle: the part could not be ejected until its slowest region was rigid, so the whole machine waited on the rib.

Two practices follow. Size ribs at 0.5 to 0.6 of the wall — 1.8 mm here — and buy stiffness with rib height and count rather than thickness, since bending stiffness goes as the cube of depth and a taller thin rib beats a thicker short one. And treat any local thickening as a cycle-time decision as well as a cosmetic one: the slowest-cooling point in the part sets the cycle for every cavity in the tool, so one badly proportioned feature is paid for on every shot for the life of the mould.

  • Thickness is squared outside the logarithm and temperatures sit inside it, so geometry dominates and process settings barely move the cycle.
  • 3 mm wall: 14.4 s cooling, 23.4 s cycle, 154 parts/h. 1.5 mm wall: 3.6 s, 10.6 s, 340 parts/h — 2.2 times the output from the same tool.
  • Clamp force \( =p_{\rm cav}A_{\rm proj} \): 525 kN, 53.5 tonnes for a 150×100 plate at 35 MPa.
  • The gate obeys the same cooling law and therefore sets the packing window: 1.6 s at 1.0 mm, 6.4 s at 2.0 mm — the smallest feature in the tool governing dimensional control.
  • A cold runner is 21% of every shot; a hot runner removes it at the cost of tooling, on the same crossover as Lesson 4.
  • Uniform shrinkage is a tooling calculation, \( L_{\rm mould}=L_{\rm part}/(1-s)=152.28 \) mm for a 150 mm part at 1.5%.
  • Differential shrinkage is the real problem: a filled grade shrinking 0.3% along flow and 0.9% across gives a 0.9 mm differential on a 150 mm plate, and the part bows.
  • Gate location sets the flow field, the flow sets the orientation, orientation sets the differential and the differential sets the warp — so a centre gate turns a bow into a dish.

8.lecture:
§1 · Blow moulding: the wall is decided before the mould closes

Extrusion blow moulding makes a hollow part in one step. A parison — a tube of melt — is extruded downward from an annular die; the two mould halves close on it, pinching it shut at top and bottom; and air inflates it against the cavity. It is fast, the tooling is cheap compared with injection moulding, and it is how nearly every plastic bottle is made.

The wall thickness, though, is not decided by the mould. It is decided by the parison, because inflation conserves mass.

Key relation — blow-up ratio and wall thinning

\[ \mathrm{BUR}=\frac{D_{\text{bottle}}}{D_{\text{parison}}},\qquad t_{\text{wall}}=\frac{t_{\text{parison}}}{\mathrm{BUR}} \]

A thin-walled tube expanded to a larger diameter keeps the same material per unit length, so its wall thins in proportion to how far it expanded.

A 40 mm parison with a 3.0 mm wall blown into a 100 mm bottle has \( \mathrm{BUR}=2.5 \) and ends with a 1.20 mm wall. Simple enough — until the bottle stops being a cylinder. A real bottle has a narrow neck, a wide body and often a waist, so the blow-up ratio varies along its height, and with a fixed die gap the wall varies inversely.

The diagram works a bottle running from a 30 mm neck through a 100 mm body to a 60 mm waist. At a constant 2.5 mm die gap the body ends at exactly the 1.0 mm target, the waist at 1.67 mm and the neck at 3.33 mm — a threefold variation, with most of the material sitting where the bottle needs it least and the thinnest section carrying the load.

The cure is parison programming: a servo moves the die mandrel during extrusion so the gap tracks the blow-up ratio the melt is about to meet. Here the gap must run from 0.75 mm at the neck to 2.5 mm at the body — a 3.3:1 range, executed over the few seconds the parison takes to extrude. That is the whole answer to why parison control sets bottle wall thickness: the mould only decides the shape, and every gram of wall was allocated before the mould closed.

Two other parison effects have to be managed with it. Sag: the parison hangs under its own weight, so its top thins while its bottom thickens. Swell: the melt is viscoelastic, so it leaves the die larger than the gap, exactly as in Lesson 6 — and both effects change with melt temperature and extrusion rate, which is why blow-moulding process settings are far less transferable between machines than moulders expect.

§2 · Thermoforming: the sheet is the budget

Thermoforming heats a sheet to its softening range and forms it over or into a mould with vacuum, air pressure, or a mechanical plug. The tooling is a fraction of an injection mould's cost and the cycle is short, which is why trays, lids and blister packs are made this way.

The same conservation argument applies, in area rather than in circumference.

Key relation — areal draw ratio

\[ \mathrm{DR}=\frac{A_{\text{part}}}{A_{\text{sheet}}},\qquad \bar t=\frac{t_{\text{sheet}}}{\mathrm{DR}} \]

The sheet's area is fixed by the frame; whatever surface the part needs comes from stretching it, and the average wall thins in proportion.

A 200 × 150 mm tray 60 mm deep needs \( 30{,}000 \) mm² of base plus \( 2(200+150)(60)=42{,}000 \) mm² of wall, so \( \mathrm{DR}=72{,}000/30{,}000=2.4 \), and a 1.2 mm sheet gives a 0.50 mm average wall.

Average is the operative word. The sheet touches the cool mould progressively, and material that has touched stops stretching, so the last regions to arrive — the corners of a deep draw — carry all the remaining strain. A corner drawing at a local ratio of 4.0 instead of the average 2.4 finishes at 0.30 mm, 40% below the average, and that corner is where the tray fails. Hence the practical depth limit of about half the width for straight vacuum forming, and hence plug assist: a plug pushes the sheet's centre down first, carrying material toward the corners before the vacuum finishes the job, which roughly doubles the achievable depth.

§3 · Film: thickness and orientation from the same two ratios

Blown film extrudes a thin tube upward through an annular die and inflates it into a bubble that is cooled, collapsed and wound. Two ratios set everything: the blow-up ratio, how far the bubble expands, and the take-up ratio, how much faster the nip rolls pull than the melt leaves.

Key relation — film thickness

\[ h_{\text{film}}=\frac{h_{\text{die}}}{\mathrm{BUR}\times\mathrm{TUR}} \]

Mass conservation again, now in two directions at once. A 1.2 mm die gap at \( \mathrm{BUR}=2.5 \) and \( \mathrm{TUR}=20 \) gives a 24 µm film.

The two ratios do something else as well, and it is what separates a good film from a bad one. The blow-up stretches the melt across the machine direction and the take-up stretches it along it, so their ratio sets how balanced the film's orientation is. At \( \mathrm{TUR}/\mathrm{BUR}=8 \) the film is strongly machine-oriented: strong and stiff along the web, and easy to tear along it too, because the molecules are aligned to split apart. A film meant to resist tearing is run at a higher blow-up ratio and a lower take-up ratio for the same thickness.

Cast film takes the other route: a flat die onto a chilled roll, which gives better clarity and much better gauge uniformity but essentially no transverse orientation, so it tears easily across the web. Neither is better; they fail differently, and the packaging decides which failure matters.

§4 · Food contact: what actually constrains the material

Packaging that touches food is regulated on what can move out of it, and that constraint reaches back into the resin, the additives and the process.

Key relations — the two migration limits

\[ m\le10\ \mathrm{mg/dm^{2}}\ \text{of contact area},\qquad m\le60\ \mathrm{mg/kg}\ \text{of food} \]

Both apply, so the binding one depends on the pack's surface-to-mass ratio. They coincide at \( A/m=6\ \mathrm{dm^{2}/kg} \); above that the mass limit binds, below it the area limit does.

A 500 ml bottle with 3.5 dm² of contact area has \( A/m=7\ \mathrm{dm^{2}/kg} \), so the mass limit binds: 30 mg of total migration is permitted, not the 35 mg the area limit would allow. Small packs, with more surface per gram of contents, are the demanding case — which is why a single-serve pot is harder to qualify than a drum of the same material.

That limit is what governs the recipe. Plasticisers, slip agents, antioxidants, stabilisers and colourants are all mobile small molecules, so a food-contact grade is chosen as much for what has been left out of it as for its mechanical properties. Recycled content is restricted for the same reason: its history is not known, so what might migrate out of it is not known either.

The second constraint is barrier, and it is a series-resistance problem identical in form to the thermal one. Polyethylene is a good moisture barrier and a poor oxygen barrier; EVOH is an excellent oxygen barrier and is ruined by moisture. So they are coextruded, with the EVOH buried between polyethylene layers, and the permeabilities add as resistances in series:

Key relation — permeation in series

\[ \frac{h_{\text{tot}}}{P_{\text{eff}}}=\sum_i\frac{h_i}{P_i} \]

Five micrometres of EVOH a thousand times less permeable than the polyethylene around it, in a 200 µm wall, cuts oxygen transmission 26-fold — from 2.5% of the wall thickness.

The third constraint is the machine rather than the material: hygienic design, meaning surfaces that can be cleaned and drained, no crevices or dead legs where product can sit, and materials that survive the cleaning chemicals. And the fourth is documentation — resin lot traceability, additive declarations and a declaration of compliance for the finished pack — which is Metrology & Quality Control's say-it, do-it, prove-it obligation appearing in another industry with different paperwork and identical logic.
